newsitem.title: MEXICO: MEXICO DEBT OUTLOOK - Higher Cetes seen as blip.
newsitem.headline: MEXICO DEBT OUTLOOK - Higher Cetes seen as blip.

text.p: Upcoming elections and another policy meeting at the Fed could bump up Mexico's Treasury bill rates in the next few weeks, but after that returns should trend lower, debt analysts said on Monday.
Markets are expected to remain wary ahead of the Open Market Committee meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve on July 2 and the upcoming July 6 elections in Mexico.
But analysts added that after the first week of July, longer-term Cetes rates in particular could show a sharp decline as economic fundamentals reassert themselves.
"I think the elections will be a pretext to exploit increases in the rates. We could see a temporary increase, but the trend is the same," Interacciones economist Alonso Cervera said.
"After (the elections) we will see fundamentals reassert themselves, and rates could drop once the elections are over," Cervera said.
The yield on the bellwether 28-day paper has risen during the past two auctions, jumping a sharp 99 basis points alone last week to 19.30 percent.
Analysts said that Banco de Mxico appears to be sanctioning slightly higher rates before early July, draining liquidity from the money markets on a regular basis.

"Banco de Mexico is saying, 'Let's play it safe, and push up rates a little before July 6,' but then we can expect a significant drop," said Alexander Anderson, an economist with brokerage house Abaco.
With the peso weakening in the past days, the higher interest rates are also seen giving support to the currency.
IDEA economist Gene Frieda said that nervousness before the polls is a good entry point for Cetes buyers, particularly as Mexico is now benefitting from a stronger balance-of-payments picture.

Economists said the fight against inflation in Mexico is paying off and price pressures should remain weak until the last few months of the year, when seasonal factors usually push up the consumer price index.
"Most people expect interest rates to continue going down with inflation," Frieda said.
Banco de Mxico was expected to report inflation of below 1.0 percent for May on Monday. That would be the first monthly number that small since the peso crash in late 1994.
As the economy grows and the government continues to clean its finances, Mexico has become a more popular bet for investors.

J.P. Morgan's emerging local markets index showed Mexico gaining 2.18 percent in May, "making it the best monthly performer for the second month in a row -- as the markets rewarded the country for its continuing economic recovery."
In July, Mexicans will vote for a new lower house in Congress, part of the upper house, governors in several states, and a mayor for Mexico City.

While an opposition candidate is expected to become the new mayor of Mexico City, it is not as clear that the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) will give up control of the lower house of Congress.
